Volume 14 · Chapter 11

Quantitative solution and model evaluation

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v14-c10

By the endAssess macroeconomic models through transparent estimation and numerical diagnostics.

Quantitative solution and model evaluation

Capability. Build and evaluate a macroeconomic model whose solution error, observation model, parameter identification and predictive failures are separately visible. The prerequisite is international macro-finance; use the verified Bellman tools in recursive methods, the local-versus-exact distinction in stochastic growth, and the inference contracts in GMM and likelihood.

A model matches an output variance and its solver reports a change below one millionth. Neither observation tells us whether the policy is feasible away from its expansion point, whether the solver maximized over the actual action set, whether two parameters produce the same moment, or whether an observation forecast improves outside the fitting sample. We will construct small economies for which those questions have exact answers. Their size makes an independent audit possible; their conclusions do not certify a larger model by analogy.

The workflow is sequential: write economic timing and ownership; state the solution and observation domains; derive a candidate; check its equations and an appropriate global or local certificate; identify parameters under an explicit sampling law; reserve validation targets; report sensitivity to parameters, numerical choices and mechanisms. A failure at one stage cannot be repaired by a higher score at another.

1. An approximation needs a domain

Begin with a household that owns a production technology, supplies fixed labor, has initial capital k₀>0, and maximizes Σβᵗlog cₜ. Full depreciation and a single good give cₜ+kₜ₊₁≤Akₜᵅ, with A>0, 0<α,β<1 and nonnegative next capital. There are no outside claims, government, debt or unfinanced investment. Capital is a goods stock; c and output are goods per model period. We normalize the utility argument by a fixed consumption unit; changing that unit adds a constant to value, not to the policy.

Let s=αβ. The exact saving policy is g(k)=sAkᵅ, consumption (1−s)Akᵅ. To derive it, insert V(k)=B log k+H into the Bellman maximand. Its k′-dependent part is log(Akᵅ−k′)+βB log k′. The derivative strictly decreases through zero, with utility tending to −∞ at either endpoint; the unique maximum has k′=βB Akᵅ/(1+βB). Matching the log-k coefficient gives B=α/(1−αβ), hence s. Matching constants gives H=[log((1−s)A)+βB log(sA)]/(1−β).

Verification, not just substitution. Candidate log capital follows xₜ₊₁=αxₜ+log(sA), so it stays bounded from each positive initial k and has finite discounted utility. Feasible alternatives have kₜ≤max{k₀,A^(1/(1−α))}; their positive utility parts are bounded and their objectives are well-defined extended real numbers. At the candidate λₜ=1/cₜ and λₜ=βλₜ₊₁αAkₜ₊₁^(α−1). Concavity of utility and production bounds any finite-horizon utility gain by −βᵀλ*T(kT+1−k*T+1) after telescoping the dated budgets. Nonnegative alternative capital bounds this above by βᵀs/(1−s), which vanishes. Thus every feasible alternative has no larger infinite-horizon value; strict concavity excludes a different consumption path attaining the same value. No lower bound on an alternative's log capital is being silently imposed. This is the accepted growth verification specialized to fixed labor; it is not an existence proof for all stochastic growth models.

The positive steady capital is k̄=(sA)^(1/(1−α)). In relative level deviations h=k/k̄−1, the exact next relative level is (1+h)ᵅ. Its first and second perturbations are 1+αh and 1+αh+α(α−1)h²/2. For |h|≤d<1, Taylor's theorem gives the explicit second-order remainder

|(1+h)ᵅ−1−αh−α(α−1)h²/2| ≤ α(1−α)(2−α)|h|³/[6(1−d)^(3−α)].

The third derivative is α(α−1)(α−2)(1+h)^(α−3); its absolute maximum on [−d,d] is the displayed coefficient. The first-order bound analogously is α(1−α)h²/[2(1−d)^(2−α)]. The interval must stay away from −1, where derivatives can diverge. Multiplying relative error by k̄ restores goods units. A pathwise claim additionally needs the exact and approximate iterations to remain within the chosen interval. A one-step Taylor bound by itself does not establish that.

Coordinate choice matters. With ℓ=log(k/k̄), the policy is exactly ℓ′=αℓ; no local truncation is needed. Exponentiating that solution recovers the nonlinear level policy, whereas exponentiating a truncated stochastic approximation can change its order and its moments. A general perturbation method differentiates the equilibrium equations around a specified steady state, selects an admissible stable solution and solves coefficient equations order by order. The solvability, stable-root and remainder hypotheses must be checked for that system. We prove a full remainder only for this explicit benchmark; we do not infer one from a small shock label or from a generic software order setting.

Worked case 1 — a precise local success and a distant failure

Take (α,β,A)=(1/2,1/2,4). Then (s,k̄,B)=(1/4,1,2/3), H=2 log 3, g(k)=√k and c(k)=3√k. For (h,d)=(1/4,1/4), exact next capital, first and second approximations are (1.118033988750,1.125,1.1171875). Their signed errors, approximation minus exact, are (0.006966011250,-0.000846488750). The second-order error certificate is 0.002004688435, which is larger than the actual absolute error.

At k=100, exact and first-order choices and available output are (10,50.5,40). The linearized policy demands more investment than the household owns and is infeasible. Calling its Euler residual small at k̄ cannot repair this. The log-coordinate policy remains exact for every positive k in this special model.

2. A global solution with a real action boundary

Now change the economy deliberately. A household owns a technology and uses linear utility in consumption. Productivity z is observed before investment and takes values L,H with AL=5 and AH=7. The exogenous transition matrix is P=((1−p,p),(q,1−q)), initially 0<p,q<1. Inherited capital k and chosen next capital a lie in [1,4]. All capital depreciates; c=Az√k−a and discount β=1/2. Since c≥5−4=1, every allowed action is resource feasible at every state. The capital bounds are economic capacity/minimum-scale constraints, not a numerical device. No firm or government pays for investment outside the household budget. An alternative may choose a using the whole observed history but never future z. Utility is consumption units per period, and value is discounted consumption units.

For a bounded continuous pair vz(k), define Tvz(k)=maxa∈[1,4]{Az√k−a+βΣPzz′vz′(a)}. Continuity and compact actions give an attained maximum. The inequality |max f−max g|≤max|f−g| and stochastic row sums imply ‖Tv−Tw‖∞≤β‖v−w‖∞. Iterating from any continuous bounded v produces a uniformly Cauchy sequence: successive differences are at most βⁿ‖Tv−v‖∞, whose geometric tail vanishes. Uniform limits remain continuous; passing through the contraction gives a fixed point, and the same inequality proves uniqueness. Bounded rewards make the terminal value term vanish under every feasible history policy. Iterating the Bellman inequality gives an upper bound on every such policy's value. An explicit continuous maximizing policy below attains equality. Thus the fixed point is the actual infinite-horizon optimum, not simply a vector produced by iteration.

The structure makes a global basis exact: Vz(k)=Az√k+Hz. Let e=P A, so eL=5+2p and eH=7−2q. The action problem is Fz(a)=−a+βez√a. Its derivative −1+βe/(2√a) strictly decreases, so the unique global choice is a*=clip((βe/2)²,1,4). Clipping means selecting the nearer active endpoint if the unconstrained maximizer is outside. Set dz=Fz(a*); then H=d+βPH, with inverse (I−βP)⁻¹=ΣβʲPʲ, a nonnegative matrix with row sums 1/(1−β). For the maintained A and β all e∈[5,7] give an interior a*∈[25/16,49/16], so d=a*.

This is a global continuous-action solution, including all k in the compact domain, because the basis identity was proved. It does not follow that a small arbitrary basis is exact in another economy. With a generic basis, evaluate the residual across the continuous state/action domain or establish an interpolation and action-search bound. Agreement only at collocation nodes is insufficient. Smooth policies can also become nondifferentiable when a capacity or borrowing constraint changes regime; a derivative reported on one side does not describe the other.

Worked case 2 — exact global policy and an economical coarse restriction

Use (β,AL,AH,p,q)=(1/2,5,7,3/10,2/5). The global choices are (49/25,961/400); H=(13859/3400,15629/3400). In state order (L,1),(L,4),(H,1),(H,4), values are (30859/3400,47859/3400,39429/3400,63229/3400). These are levels of discounted consumption, not prices of traded securities.

Restrict an approximate solver's investment choices to G={1,4}, leaving the true economy unchanged. The difference F(4)−F(1)=−3+βe gives coarse choices (1,4), with dG=(9/5,11/5) and HG=(318/85,358/85). The approximate value VGz(k)=Az√k+HGz solves its restricted Bellman equation exactly everywhere in k. The coarse policy is feasible in the original economy and its actual value is VG; it simply leaves attainable consumption value unexploited.

3. Turn approximation error into an auditable bound

For any bounded candidate v, δ=‖Tv−v‖∞ implies ‖v−V‖∞≤δ/(1−β), by inserting Tv and using the contraction. If an approximate operator T̃ supplies residual δ̂ and a separately established error ‖T̃v−Tv‖∞≤εB, replace δ by δ̂+εB. εB may contain quadrature, action-search, interpolation and roundoff contributions; it is not estimated by the final iteration difference. Separate theoretical error bounds from floating-point checks.

A feasible σ with 0≤Tv−Tσv≤η has ‖v−Vσ‖∞≤(δ+η)/(1−β), by its own policy contraction. Hence 0≤V−Vσ and its sup norm is at most (2δ+η)/(1−β). This deliberately conservative bound needs both value and greediness errors. When v is exactly the value of σ and Tv−v≥0, the sharper δ/(1−β) bound already bounds the policy loss. A zero residual for T̃ says nothing about T unless their discrepancy is controlled.

Action-grid certificate. For the separable economy, F′(a)=−1+βe/(2√a). On [1,4] and e∈[5,7] its absolute value is at most 3/4. A grid including both endpoints with maximum gap h has a node within h/2 of the continuous maximizer. The mean-value theorem bounds the lost action reward by 3h/8. Here the maximizer is interior and F′(a*)=0; since |F″|=βe/(4a^(3/2))≤7/8, Taylor's theorem improves the loss to 7h²/64. Solve the restricted constant equation accurately and divide that action loss by 1−β to bound the resulting value loss. The quadratic bound uses the zero derivative; if the maximizer is at a boundary included in the grid, the loss is zero instead. In another model, a omitted endpoint or an unbounded derivative defeats this argument.

Primitive sensitivity is a different error. Consider two otherwise comparable bounded-reward models with the same states, actions and discount, reward difference at most εr, and max row-sum absolute transition difference εP. Suppose both rewards have absolute value at most R, so both values have norm at most R/(1−β). Applying the two Bellman operators to one value and the contraction yields

‖V−Ṽ‖∞ ≤ εᵣ/(1−β)+βRε_P/(1−β)².

The transition bound follows directly from |Σ(P−P̃)Ṽ|≤εP‖Ṽ‖∞. It holds uniformly over feasible actions, including continuous choices, when the comparison uses the same reward bound and state domain. A row's total variation distance is half its absolute row sum, so switching conventions without the factor two misstates the bound. The theorem compares optimal values, not causal welfare effects or policy labels. Near a tie, a tiny primitive change can switch a discrete policy while leaving value nearly unchanged.

Worked case 3 — detect the operator the solver omitted

For VG above, its true continuous Bellman residual by productivity state is d−dG=(4/25,81/400). It is independent of k, so the domain-wide maximum is known rather than sampled. The value/policy loss certificate is 81/200. Solving (I−βP)(H−HG)=d−dG gives actual losses (67/200,77/200), whose maximum is below the bound. Reporting the restricted residual zero as an exact solution would hide this loss.

A uniform grid with h=1/4 has action-loss bound 7/1024 and value-loss bound 7/512 before any iteration or roundoff error. For a transition scenario with |Δp|,|Δq|≤1/20, εP≤1/10. Consumption rewards are between 1 and 13, so R=13; the generic primitive-value bound is 13/5. This loose bound cannot be reported as sampling uncertainty unless a statistical procedure justifies the parameter region.

4. The observation design determines the likelihood

We now treat p,q as unknown, keeping the technology, capacity and preference primitives fixed. These data are synthetic. Imagine independent economies observed for one transition each. Sampling fixes nL economies initially in L and nH initially in H; transitions are independent across economies conditional on those assigned initial states and share the same p,q. A switch indicator in the L group is Bernoulli(p); in the H group it is Bernoulli(q). Initial-state proportions are design choices, not observations from the stationary distribution. Complete observation of z and common transition parameters are substantive assumptions; measurement error, hidden states or correlated shocks require a different likelihood.

With switch counts mL,mH, the likelihood for ordered observations, apart from parameter-free terms when counts alone are observed, has log

ℓ(p,q)=m_L log p+(n_L−m_L)log(1−p)+m_H log q+(n_H−m_H)log(1−q).

For 0<m<n, the one-parameter derivative is (m−nx)/[x(1−x)] and changes from positive to negative at x=m/n. Thus the global unique interior maximum is the sample switch fraction, with negative second derivative −m/x²−(n−m)/(1−x)². If m=0 or n, the likelihood is monotone on the open interval and has only a boundary supremum; a constrained closed-domain model attains it at 0 or 1. If n=0 the row parameter is unidentified by these data. These distinctions matter when stationarity formulas below demand interior transitions. Adding pseudo-counts changes the objective or prior; it is not the unpenalized MLE.

For the stated independent panel design, E p̂=p and Var(p̂)=p(1−p)/nL, similarly for q̂, and the two estimates are independent. To prove this, sum independent Bernoulli indicators, each with mean x and variance x(1−x), then divide by n². Plug-in standard errors estimate those variances, not exact confidence coverage. For any ε>0, Markov's inequality applied to (p̂−p)² gives Pr(|p̂−p|≥ε)≤p(1−p)/(nLε²)≤1/(4nLε²). The union bound gives simultaneous error probability at most (1/nL+1/nH)/(4ε²), capped at one. This conservative finite-sample statement needs no asymptotic normal approximation. Inverting exact binomial tails would give a different, usually tighter procedure.

For one long observed Markov path, multiplying conditional transition probabilities produces the same count expression conditional on its initial state. That algebra does not make realized visits to each origin a fixed independent-binomial sample: visits and transitions are linked. Its consistency, central limit theorem and uncertainty estimates require an appropriate Markov/dependence argument, absent here. Likewise adding a stationary initial-density term changes an unconditional path likelihood. Use the panel result only for the panel design actually stated.

Worked case 4 — estimate transitions, then separate three sources of sensitivity

The training counts (nL,mL,nH,mH) are (20,6,20,8). Their MLE is (3/10,2/5), which supplied worked case 2. Plug-in standard errors are (0.102469507660,0.109544511501). These are small synthetic groups; neither the number of decimal places nor the exact global solve makes the parameter estimates precise.

In an interior regime aL=(β(5+2p)/2)² and aH=(β(7−2q)/2)². Differentiation gives (∂aL/∂p,∂aH/∂q)=(7/5,-31/20) at the estimate. Raising p by 1/10 changes the low-state choice to 841/400, a change 57/400. The first-order change is 7/50; the difference 1/400 is the exact quadratic term. This parameter scenario is distinct from the k-domain Taylor truncation in case 1 and the action-grid restriction in case 3.

For illustration, independent groups with sizes (200,200,1/5), listing nL,nH,ε, have a simultaneous Chebyshev error bound 1/16. This is a hypothetical sampling guarantee before observing that larger sample, not a retrospective claim about the twenty-observation groups above. A scenario rectangle [0.2,0.4]×[0.3,0.5] has no stated confidence level; the coarse high-state action reaches a tie at q=0.5 even while the continuous policy varies smoothly.

5. A fitted moment is not an identified parameter

Let Xₜ indicate high productivity in a stationary two-state chain with 0<p,q<1. Stationarity solves μ=(1−μ)p+μ(1−q), giving μ=p/(p+q). The conditional mean is E[Xₜ₊₁|Xₜ]=p+(1−p−q)Xₜ. Define ρ=1−p−q∈(−1,1). Then E[Xₜ₊₁−μ|Xₜ]=ρ(Xₜ−μ), so multiplying by Xₜ−μ and averaging gives Cov(Xₜ,Xₜ₊₁)=ρμ(1−μ). This proves the one-lag correlation formula because μ∈(0,1). The mean and covariance refer to a stationary chain, not to the fixed initial proportions in our conditional panel.

Matching μ alone identifies a curve, not a point: for any scale t>0 with μt<1 and (1−μ)t<1, p=μt,q=(1−μ)t gives the same mean. With both μ and ρ, inversion is p=μ(1−ρ),q=(1−μ)(1−ρ), subject to both lying in (0,1). The Jacobian of (μ,ρ) with respect to (p,q) has rows (q/(p+q)²,−p/(p+q)²) and (−1,−1), hence determinant −1/(p+q)≠0. Here the explicit inverse proves global identification; full local rank alone would not prove global identification in an arbitrary nonlinear model.

A moment estimator minimizes [m̂−m(θ)]ᵀW[m̂−m(θ)] over a declared feasible parameter domain with positive definite W. If the two empirical targets invert to an interior p,q, their zero discrepancy is the unique global minimizer for any such W. If they do not, there is no exact match and weighting affects the projection; report the unmatched moments and constraints. If only μ is targeted, no positive weight can eliminate its identified curve. Correlated sample moments require their joint covariance for statistical weighting. Adding redundant transforms of the same moment does not create information. A simulation-based moment estimator also has finite simulation error; common random numbers can make comparisons less noisy but cannot create identification or turn a pseudorandom seed into an uncertainty theorem.

Worked case 5 — the same stationary average, different persistence and policy

The fitted parameters imply (μ,ρ,Var X,Cov(Xₜ,Xₜ₊₁))=(3/7,3/10,12/49,18/245). The alternative pair (3/20,1/5) implies (3/7,13/20,12/49,39/245). The stationary high fraction and variance match exactly, but persistence does not: adding the indicator variance μ(1−μ) did not provide a new independent restriction.

With the alternative transitions, global investment choices become (2809/1600,1089/400). Thus fitting the same average productivity, 5+2μ, can leave a different dynamic policy. The Jacobian determinant at the training estimate is -10/7. Neither that nonzero determinant nor the perfect fit establishes that the two-state technology is a true account of measured macroeconomic data.

6. Validation asks questions that estimation did not answer

Before fitting, record the transformation and vintage of the observable, the training/validation split, the economic mechanism under test and the loss used for comparison. Reserve outcomes or horizons that could contradict the model: transition persistence, cross-covariances, responses in different states, policy feasibility near constraints, or a held-out predictive distribution. A model that matches exactly as many independent moments as parameters has no spare fit restriction in those targets. A likelihood-ratio, moment or forecast test needs its own sampling calibration, especially after selecting specifications. A synthetic benchmark can detect algorithmic failure but is not empirical validation.

For a Bernoulli switch forecast x and realized indicator y, the log score is y log x+(1−y)log(1−x); a larger score is better. If the actual switch probability is t∈(0,1), its expected derivative in x is (t−x)/[x(1−x)], so truthful x=t uniquely maximizes expected score. Equivalently the excess expected loss is t log(t/x)+(1−t)log((1−t)/(1−x))≥0 by that maximization. The Brier loss (y−x)² has expectation t(1−t)+(x−t)², also uniquely minimized at truth. These are population propriety results; a finite realized score can favor an incorrect forecast. Giving probability zero to a realized switch produces negative infinite log score, which is a substantive forecasting failure, not a missing value to discard.

The independent validation groups contain counts (10,5,10,2). Compare the fitted (0.3,0.4) with a prespecified calibration (1/4,1/4). Training average log scores (fit,calibration) are (-0.641937984532,-0.672196373486); validation scores are (-0.686121259760,-0.672196373486). Training Brier losses are (9/40,19/80); validation losses are (49/200,19/80). The fitted model wins in sample and loses on this small holdout by both measures. This illustrates the distinction, not statistically significant superiority of the calibration. Refit on the holdout and it ceases to be an untouched holdout; reserve another evaluation or acknowledge selection.

A practical sensitivity table should distinguish numerical refinement with fixed primitives; local parameter derivatives and finite scenarios; sampling uncertainty under a named design; structural changes such as risk aversion, adjustment costs, partial depreciation or hidden productivity; and observable definitions. Compare consumption or welfare only under common ownership, financing and initial-state conventions. Our linear-utility compact investment problem and log-utility unbounded-state growth problem are different laboratories, not two calibrations of one welfare metric.

Reproducible protocol. Store primitive inputs, units and state/action ordering. Keep a slow benchmark that directly solves the small problem. Evaluate residuals with the original operator, then add arithmetic/search bounds if a formal numerical certificate is claimed. Record every unsupported boundary and the norm used. For estimation, retain synthetic counts or the actual legally usable observation table and its transformation code, the parameter domain, objective and convergence diagnostics. Report identification before a covariance matrix. For validation, preserve the prespecified score and split; for sensitivity, name which assumption changed. The standard-library checker accompanying this chapter reconstructs the displayed witnesses; it does not claim a generic exact real-arithmetic certificate for arbitrary floating-point models.

7. Exercises and complete solutions

  1. Derive the saving fraction and value coefficients for the log-growth economy without assuming an Euler equation is sufficient. Prove the candidate globally optimal against all feasible history-independent alternatives and explain why zero capital is outside its positive-initial-state statement. Reproduce case 1's two approximations, errors and bound. Prove the exact, first-order and second-order relative policies each map [−1/4,1/4] into itself in that example.
  2. For the compact investment economy, prove the global Bellman fixed point is actual value for every feasible history policy. Derive the clipped optimizer for arbitrary β>0 and expected productivity e>0, state both endpoint conditions, then specialize to the chapter's discount and productivity domain. Explain why evaluating a basis only at two capital nodes would not ordinarily prove it exact.
  3. Independently solve the two linear constant equations in case 2, for both the full interval and G={1,4}. Verify all four displayed global values and both optimal grid actions. Derive the true residual of the restricted-policy value over the whole continuous state domain and compare exact value loss with its certificate.
  4. Prove both the general approximate-greedy policy bound and the sharper bound for an exact policy value. An approximate continuous Bellman evaluation has residual δ̂=1/1000 and known uniform operator error εB=1/500; its feasible policy has true greediness defect η≤1/200, with β=1/2. Bound value error and policy regret. Explain which conclusion fails if εB is merely an unverified guess.
  5. Derive the Lipschitz and second-derivative action-grid certificates, retaining the half-gap factor. Compute the two value bounds for h=1/4 and β=1/2. Explain why a grid that omits the domain endpoint can lose at a constrained optimum, and how the proof changes if the derivative is unbounded.
  6. Derive the transition/reward sensitivity theorem from the original operators. Explain the factor two between absolute row sum and total variation. In the coarse action set, vary q from 49/100 to 51/100 holding p fixed. Find the signed advantage of action 4 over action 1 in each case and the tie at q=1/2. Contrast the policy-label discontinuity with continuity of value and of the unrestricted optimal action.
  7. Derive the panel likelihood, its unique interior maximizer and all m=0,m=n,n=0 cases. Reproduce the training estimates and plug-in standard errors. Prove the simultaneous Chebyshev bound for the stated independent two-group design and recompute case 4. Explain precisely why the same count likelihood for one Markov path does not justify the same fixed-n binomial variance calculation.
  8. Prove the stationary mean/covariance formulas and the complete identified curve under a mean target. Derive the two-moment inverse and Jacobian determinant; state its feasible image. Recompute the alternative pair's moments and policy. Explain why adding the indicator variance to the mean supplies no new identification.
  9. Suppose a researcher targets (μ,ρ)=(4/5,−1/2). Invert them and diagnose whether an interior two-state transition model can match exactly. Explain the role of a positive-definite GMM weight when no exact feasible match exists. Derive the local investment sensitivity and finite p-change in case 4, including the quadratic remainder.
  10. Prove expected log-score and Brier optimality. Recompute both training and validation comparisons and distinguish a finite ranking from a calibrated statistical test. What happens to log scoring if an x=0 forecast observes a switch? Why is choosing the comparator after inspecting validation outcomes a change in the evaluation design?
  11. A code returns the exact restricted value from case 2, labels its residual zero, and reports “the continuous economy is solved globally.” Give two independent diagnostics that refute that statement, with numbers. Then explain how a residual can be nonzero after rounding a truly exact solution and what additional arithmetic analysis a rigorous machine-level certificate requires. Distinguish validation at collocation nodes from a supremum over all states.
  12. Referee a paper claiming: “A second-order solver converged, three moments fit two parameters, and in-sample likelihood increased, so the policy intervention is identified and welfare improving.” Write a defensible replacement claim and a minimal reproducible evaluation plan. Identify missing numerical, statistical and economic assumptions. Use the rubric below to assess the argument, not its agreement with a favored policy.
Complete solutions and proof checks

  1. The log-k coefficient satisfies B=α(1+βB), so B=α/(1−αβ), and the unique derivative zero gives s=βB/(1+βB)=αβ. Matching constants gives the stated H. Candidate log capital is a stable affine recursion; candidate consumption remains positive and its discounted log utility is finite. Feasible capital is uniformly bounded above, so positive utility parts are summable for every alternative. Concavity yields the telescoping finite-horizon tangent bound βᵀs/(1−s)→0, proving global optimality even when an alternative's value is −∞. The argument assumes k₀>0: at k₀=0, production and feasible consumption are zero forever and log utility is −∞, so the positive-state value formula cannot be substituted there.

    For α=1/2, h=1/4, the polynomials give 9/8 and 143/128, while the exact choice is √5/2; subtract it and apply the third-derivative bound to reproduce case 1. For invariance, each map is increasing on [−1/4,1/4]. Exact next h lies between √(3/4)−1 and √(5/4)−1, both inside the interval. The first-order map h/2 has endpoints ±1/8. The second-order map h/2−h²/8 has endpoints −17/128 and 15/128, inside the interval; its derivative 1/2−h/4 is positive there. This supports repeated use of that interval's one-step bound. It does not imply errors never accumulate; a separate stability estimate is needed to bound path differences.

  2. Compact [1,4] and continuous bounded rewards give attained Bellman maxima. The max inequality and probability row sums give contraction β. The geometric bound on successive iterates proves uniform convergence to a continuous fixed point; contraction makes it unique. Iterate its Bellman inequality along any admissible history strategy; bounded V makes βᵀE V vanish, so no strategy beats V. The explicit continuous maximizing rule attains equality at every history, and therefore attains V. No generic measurable selection theorem is being presumed without need.

    F′(a)=−1+βe/(2√a), F″(a)=−βe/(4a^(3/2))<0. If βe≤2 the optimum is 1; if βe≥4 it is 4; otherwise it is (βe/2)². At equality the unconstrained optimum equals the endpoint and remains unique. The derivative computation is valid for β>0, but an infinite-horizon bounded-value contraction additionally requires β<1. Here βe∈[5/2,7/2], so all optima are interior. Substitution makes the entire k dependence exactly Az√k on both sides. Two collocation equalities alone would leave all between-node errors uncontrolled without that identity.

  3. For any d, (1−β+βp)HL−βpHH=dL and −βqHL+(1−β+βq)HH=dH. Their determinant is (1−β)[1−β+β(p+q)]>0. The interior actions and d are 49/25 and 961/400. Inverting gives H=(13859/3400,15629/3400); adding 5,10 or 7,14 gives all four values printed in case 2. For the coarse problem, advantages −3+βe are −1/5 and 1/10, hence actions 1 and 4. The immediate constant terms are 9/5 and 11/5, yielding HG=(318/85,358/85).

    Applying the true operator to VG replaces only dG with d; all k dependence cancels. Thus the residual is (4/25,81/400) at every k. The nonnegative inverse gives losses (67/200,77/200); their maximum 77/200≤81/200 certifies the comparison. Both the restricted value equation and the exact policy-value equation hold, so the loss is economic opportunity loss caused by the restricted action set, not an infeasible trade.

  4. Insert Tv between v and V to get E≤δ+βE. For a policy with greediness defect at most η, ‖Tσv−v‖≤δ+η, hence its policy-value error is at most (δ+η)/(1−β). The triangle inequality gives regret at most (2δ+η)/(1−β); feasible optimality gives the nonnegative sign. If v=Vσ exactly, the first value bound is already a policy-loss bound and no triangle addition is needed. With operator error, δ≤δ̂+εB=3/1000. The value and general policy-loss bounds are (3/500,11/500). If εB is unverified, the number is only a conditional calculation; neither it nor the solver's tolerance establishes a true-operator error certificate.

  5. The extreme derivative values over e∈[5,7],a∈[1,4] lie between −3/8 and 3/4, giving |F′|≤3/4. A nearest node is within h/2, so loss≤3h/8. At an interior maximizer F′=0 and |F″|≤7/8 gives loss≤(1/2)(7/8)(h/2)²=7h²/64. Divide each by 1−β: for h=1/4 the two value bounds are (3/16,7/512). At a constrained maximizer that is included as a grid endpoint the loss is zero. If it is omitted, the nearest-point geometry must be recomputed and the nonzero endpoint derivative typically produces first-order rather than second-order error. An unbounded derivative invalidates the stated uniform constants; a narrower domain or a separately proved modulus of continuity is required.

  6. Subtract fixed-point equations, insert TṼ, and use contraction for the value difference. The remaining operator difference is bounded by εr+βεP‖Ṽ‖, and bounded rewards give ‖Ṽ‖≤R/(1−β). Rearrangement gives the displayed bound. For a two-state row changed by Δp, both entries change in absolute value |Δp|, so the row sum is 2|Δp| while total variation is |Δp|.

    The coarse high-state advantage is 1/2−q, giving (1/100,-1/100,0) at q=49/100,51/100,1/2 respectively. Thus the strict coarse optimizer switches from 4 to 1 and both are optimal at the tie. The maximum of continuous action values and the bounded inverse evaluation remain continuous in parameters; the sensitivity theorem quantifies that continuity. The unrestricted optimizer ((7−2q)/4)² remains smooth across q=1/2 because it stays inside [1,4]. Policy labels need not inherit smoothness from values.

  7. Conditional independence multiplies the Bernoulli factors. The derivative (m−nx)/[x(1−x)] proves the interior global optimum m/n. All-zero counts give a strictly decreasing likelihood on (0,1), all-one counts a strictly increasing one; each has a supremum but no maximum on that open domain. On [0,1] use the usual continuous probability limits and obtain boundary maxima. No origin observations gives a constant likelihood in that row parameter. The specified counts give p̂=3/10,q̂=2/5 and the printed square roots of (21/100)/20 and (6/25)/20.

    Independence gives Var(mean)=x(1−x)/n. Markov's inequality for squared deviation and x(1−x)≤1/4 give each tail bound; summing the two bounds gives the simultaneous result, without assuming the tail events independent. At nL=nH=200,ε=1/5, it is 1/16. A realized Markov path's origin counts are random and linked to earlier transitions. Conditioning on the entire origin schedule does not generally preserve independent Bernoulli successors. The path likelihood remains correct, but the finite-panel variance proof no longer applies.

  8. Stationary balance gives μq=(1−μ)p and μ=p/(p+q). Conditional mean p+(1−p−q)X gives the centered regression with coefficient ρ, so covariance is ρVar X=ρμ(1−μ). All mean-equivalent pairs are (μt,(1−μ)t), with 0<t<min{1/μ,1/(1−μ)}. A second independent persistence target fixes t=1−ρ. The feasible moment image is 0<μ<1 and 0<μ(1−ρ)<1,0<(1−μ)(1−ρ)<1; these inequalities imply −1<ρ<1 but are stronger for means far from one half.

    The derivative rows in the text have determinant −1/(p+q), giving −10/7 at the fit. For p=3/20,q=1/5, t=7/20, μ=3/7,ρ=13/20 and variance12/49 give covariance39/245. Expected productivities are 53/10 and 33/5, so investment is (53/40)²=2809/1600 and (33/20)²=1089/400. Indicator variance is fixed by μ; matching it again cannot identify the persistence scale.

  9. The inverse targets yield (6/5,3/10), so p exceeds one and no two-state transition law matches exactly. A positive-definite weighting matrix ranks nonzero discrepancies over a declared feasible domain; if an optimizer exists, its location can depend on that ranking. On an open domain a boundary infimum may fail to be attained, so numerical projection onto a closed trimmed parameter set also changes the specification.

    For an interior low-state action a=(5+2p)²/16, a′=(5+2p)/4 and a″=1/2. At p=3/10, a′=7/5. A change Δp=1/10 gives Δa=(7/5)(1/10)+(1/4)(1/10)²=57/400, of which 1/400 is the quadratic term; new a=841/400. For high productivity a=(7−2q)²/16, its derivative is −(7−2q)/4=−31/20. These are comparative statics under fixed estimated model primitives, not sampling confidence intervals or identified causal policy effects.

  10. For actual t, expected log score is t log x+(1−t)log(1−x); the derivative changes sign at t and the score tends to −∞ at either endpoint for interior t. Thus t is its unique maximizer. Expanding E(Y−x)² gives Var Y+(EY−x)²=t(1−t)+(t−x)², proving the Brier result. Sum the successes' and failures' scores with each group's forecast and divide by total observations to obtain the four log scores and four Brier values in section 6.

    The fit improves training averages, while the prespecified calibration improves this validation realization. Neither rank is a significance statement without a sampling comparison, dependence assumptions and any model-selection correction. If x=0 and y=1, log score is −∞ and the forecast assigns zero probability to an observed event; deleting that observation changes the evaluation. Choosing a comparator after seeing validation outcomes uses those outcomes for selection, so the comparison is exploratory unless evaluated on fresh data or under an explicit selection-adjusted design.

  11. First evaluate the continuous action (49/25,961/400) in the original maximand: it improves the one-step choices over the grid by (4/25,81/400), so the true residual cannot be zero. Second solve the exact continuous constant equations and compare value functions: the global gains are (67/200,77/200). These diagnostics use action feasibility and policy value, not the solver's reported stopping rule. Both apply at every k because the basis dependence is exact.

    Rounding H perturbs both sides of its linear equation and can create a residual even if the unrounded expression is exact. A rigorous machine-level bound would need directed/interval rounding or a justified accumulation bound for the arithmetic, linear solve and maximization, plus coverage of the entire state/action domain. The chapter checker uses rational arithmetic for the certificates and numerical tolerance for log/square-root displays; it does not claim that arbitrary floating-point code inherits formal interval bounds. Testing a finite set of collocation nodes alone cannot exclude a between-node residual spike.

  12. A defensible replacement is: “In the stated economy and approximation domain, this candidate meets these numerical error bounds. The chosen observation model identifies these parameter combinations under these assumptions. It fits these training targets and has these prespecified validation scores; welfare comparisons are conditional on the stated ownership, financing and initial state.” Request the equations and timing, full feasible action sets, approximation region and stability argument, original-operator residual with operator/arithmetic error, and independent small benchmark. Request raw-data provenance, transformations, observation likelihood, identification map/rank and global alternatives, sampling design and uncertainty treatment. Request untouched validation targets, score, comparator selection and sensitivity to structural mechanisms. Three counted moments may include a redundant variance; solver convergence is not model accuracy; likelihood gain is not a causal intervention; welfare requires a defined objective and budget-complete allocation.

    Twenty-point rubric. Award 4 for numerical domain/true-operator and independent diagnostic; 4 for identification, redundancy and sampling law; 4 for honest validation and selection; 4 for ownership, resource feasibility, welfare and structural sensitivity; 4 for a concrete reproducible replacement claim and evidence plan. A numerically polished causal or welfare assertion without the required identifying/economic assumptions remains a critical error. Support or rejection of the policy can both earn full credit when justified.

8. Explain, retain and extend

Teach-back. In five minutes explain why “the algorithm converged” is not a joint certificate of a policy, parameter and economic mechanism. Use the three distinct failures in this chapter: infeasible distant perturbation, zero restricted-operator residual, and mean-equivalent transition laws.

Benchmark answer

The level perturbation demands 50.5 units at capital100 while output is40, so it is infeasible outside its proved region. The exact coarse solve has zero residual only for its two-action operator; the true operator has maximum residual81/400 and the coarse policy loses up to77/200 in value. The two transition pairs have the same stationary mean3/7 but different persistence and investment choices. Correct computation, identifying observations and an appropriate mechanism are separate requirements. A held-out score adds evidence on predictive performance under its design; it does not alone identify intervention welfare.

After one week. Derive the determinant of I−βP; show how to certify a candidate with δ̂,εB; and invert a mean/persistence pair before checking its probability domain. After one month. Explain whether a coarse policy can switch discontinuously while its value changes continuously, and whether a better realized holdout score proves the forecast law true.

Retention answer key

The determinant is (1−β)[1−β+β(p+q)], strictly positive for 0<β<1 and nonnegative p,q. Value error is at most (δ̂+εB)/(1−β) only when the operator discrepancy is established. Inversion is p=μ(1−ρ),q=(1−μ)(1−ρ); both must be feasible probabilities before discussing a fit. At q=1/2 the coarse actions tie; tiny changes select different labels although bounded reward/transition perturbations bound the value change. A realized score is a sample comparison, while expected-score optimality is a statement under a specified true law; neither eliminates model-selection or sampling uncertainty.

For primary method routes, use Sargent and Stachurski's discrete dynamic programming lecture, Lorenzoni's optimal-growth notes, Chernozhukov and Fernandez-Val's GMM lecture, and Rigollet's likelihood lecture. Their previously inspected scopes are recorded in the source record; the examples, compact-domain proofs and evaluation design here are original. We have not proved a general nonlinear perturbation remainder, generic quadrature accuracy, hidden-state likelihood identification, or dependent-series inference theorem. The next planned chapter, frontiers and research proposals, uses these distinctions to build questions a model can actually answer.

Sources and further study

  • Sargent and Stachurski — QuantEcon, Discrete State Dynamic Programming — Author-led extension to stochastic finite-state Bellman problems; this library uses its own deterministic example and standard-library code.
  • Guido Lorenzoni — MIT 14.451 Lecture Notes 5: Optimal Growth Model (Fall 2009) — Owned production/consumption budget and the distinction between positive consumption, envelope conditions and Euler equations.
  • Victor Chernozhukov, Ivan Fernandez-Val — Structural Equations Models and GMM (MIT OpenCourseWare, 14.382 Econometrics, Spring2017, Lecture3) — Fixed-dimensional linear GMM, sample normal equations, covariance weighting and the 2SLS special case. Signed and dimensionally consistent formulas are independently derived.
  • 18.650 Statistics for Applications, Chapter 3: Maximum Likelihood Estimation — KL definition and information inequality, likelihood maximization, gradient/Hessian, examples, information and regular limit statement. PDF page numbers differ from the slide footers by one.
